title: Seismic waves and Earth's interior
keyIdea: An earthquake sends two kinds of wave through Earth. P waves push and pull the rock along their path, travel fastest and pass through solids and liquids. S waves shake the rock sideways, travel more slowly and cannot pass through a liquid. Because no S waves reach the far side of Earth, the outer core must be liquid. P waves bend where they enter the core, leaving a shadow zone from 104° to 140° round from the quake, and faint P waves inside that zone revealed a solid inner core. Waves, not drills, mapped Earth's layers.
familyTip: Stretch a slinky or a long spring along a table. Push one end to send a P wave, then flick it sideways to send an S wave. Ask: which one could still travel if the slinky were a tube of water, and why?

visual.caption: P wave or S wave? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort P and S waves, test them in solid and liquid, time the S minus P gap, map the shadow zones, and read Earth's layers from the clues.

kid: An earthquake sends waves through the whole Earth. Seismometers all round the world record them. There are two main kinds that travel through the inside of Earth: P waves and S waves.

A P wave pushes and pulls the rock along its path, like a squeezed spring. It is the fastest wave, so it arrives first. P stands for primary. An S wave shakes the rock from side to side, across its path. It is slower, so it arrives second. S stands for secondary.

P waves can pass through solids and liquids. S waves cannot pass through a liquid, because a liquid just flows when you shear it. The further a station is from the quake, the longer the gap between P and S. That gap tells you how far away the quake was.

No S waves arrive more than 104° round the Earth from a quake. So the outer core must be liquid. P waves bend at the core and leave a shadow zone where no direct waves arrive. Faint P waves inside that zone showed a solid inner core. Nobody has drilled deeper than about 12 km. The waves did the mapping.
adult: Ages 11 to 13. The KS3 science curriculum (DfE 2013) asks for the structure of the Earth, and GCSE Physics (AQA 8463, 4.6.1.5) asks students to explain how P and S waves give evidence for the structure and size of Earth's core. NGSS HS-ESS2-3 asks for a model of Earth's interior built from seismic evidence. Key words: seismometer, P wave, S wave, longitudinal, transverse, compression, shear, refraction, shadow zone, core-mantle boundary.

P waves are longitudinal and travel at about 6 km/s in the upper crust, rising to about 13 km/s deep in the mantle. S waves are transverse, travel at about 3.5 km/s near the surface and are roughly 0.6 times as fast as P waves. A liquid has no rigidity, so it cannot carry a shear wave. Near a quake, each second of S minus P delay means roughly 8 km of distance; three stations fix the epicentre.

Oldham found the core in 1906 and Gutenberg placed its edge near 2,900 km in 1914. Jeffreys argued in 1926 that the outer core is liquid, because S waves never arrive more than about 104° from a quake. P waves slow down and bend as they enter the core, so no direct P waves reach 104° to 140° (USGS). In 1936 Inge Lehmann explained faint P waves inside that zone with a faster, solid inner core, now known to have a radius of about 1,220 km. Wave paths in the mantle curve because speed rises with depth.

Common mistakes: swapping which wave is longitudinal and which is transverse; thinking S waves can cross liquids; thinking the S minus P gap is the same everywhere; thinking scientists have drilled to the mantle or core (the Kola borehole stopped at about 12 km); thinking the whole core is liquid, or the whole core solid; and thinking S arrives first. The lab sorts 6 facts, runs 4 solid and liquid tests, matches 3 S minus P gaps to distances, maps 3 zones on a cut-through Earth and matches 4 clues to conclusions.

practice.prompt: Which wave cannot travel through a liquid?
practice.hint: Which wave shakes the rock sideways?
practice.explain: The S wave is a shear wave. A liquid flows instead of passing on a sideways shake, so S waves stop.

practice.prompt: A seismometer records the S wave {a} seconds after the P wave. Using about 8 km for every second of gap, how far away was the quake?
practice.hint: Multiply the gap in seconds by 8 km.

practice.prompt: A P wave travels at 6 km/s through the crust. How many seconds does it take to reach a station {=6*a} km away?
practice.hint: Time = distance ÷ speed. Divide the distance by 6.

practice.prompt: Where on Earth's surface do no direct P or S waves arrive from a quake?
choices: Between 104° and 140° round from the quake
Exactly on the opposite side, at 180°
practice.hint: Think of the red rim in the lab.
practice.explain: Between 104° and 140° is the shadow zone. Beyond 140° P waves arrive again, after crossing the core.

practice.prompt: Faint P waves arrive inside the shadow zone. What did Inge Lehmann conclude in 1936?
choices: There is a solid inner core
The shadow zone does not exist
practice.hint: Something inside the core bent those waves.
practice.explain: A faster, solid inner core bends some P waves into the shadow zone. That was Lehmann's discovery.

pool.prompt: In a P wave, which way does the rock move?
choices: Back and forth along the path of the wave
Up and down, across the path
pool.explain: The rock is squeezed and stretched along the direction of travel. That is a longitudinal, compression wave.

pool.prompt: Deep in the mantle an S wave travels at about 7 km/s. How far does it travel in {a} seconds?
pool.hint: Distance = speed × time. Multiply 7 by the seconds.

pool.prompt: Station B records an S minus P gap {a} seconds longer than station A. Using about 8 km per second of gap, how much further from the quake is B?
pool.hint: Each extra second of gap is about 8 km more.

pool.prompt: Why do no S waves reach the side of Earth far from a quake?
choices: The liquid outer core stops them
They run out of energy at the surface
pool.hint: Which state of matter stops a shear wave?
pool.explain: S waves cannot cross a liquid, and the outer core is liquid. That is how we know it is liquid.

pool.prompt: Why is the P wave called the primary wave?
choices: It only travels in the crust
pool.hint: Look at the order on the seismometer trace.
pool.explain: P waves are the fastest, so they are the first, or primary, waves to arrive.

pool.prompt: The deepest hole ever drilled is about 12 km. How do we know the outer core is liquid?
choices: From how earthquake waves travel through Earth
From rock drilled up from the core
pool.hint: The core starts about 2,900 km down.
pool.explain: No drill reaches the core. S waves cannot cross it, so it must be liquid.

pool.prompt: Why does a P wave shadow zone exist?
choices: P waves bend as they enter the core
The mantle absorbs all P waves
pool.hint: P waves do cross the core, but their path changes.
pool.explain: P waves slow down and bend (refract) at the core-mantle boundary, so none arrive directly between 104° and 140°.

pool.prompt: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
pool.hint: Think about where S waves stop.
pool.explain: The outer core is liquid metal. The inner core is solid, and so are the crust and nearly all of the mantle.
